changes.before: Add input.add(1) inside total. Why is the changed program rejected?
changes.after: Use wildcards to say what a method can safely read or add.

before: List<? extends Number> accepts a List<Integer> for reading as Number values. The ? stands for an unknown particular type. You cannot safely add an arbitrary non-null Number: the actual list might require Integer.

List<? super Integer> can receive Integer values; its actual element type is Integer or a supertype. Reading from that unknown list gives only Object without additional checks. The mnemonic is producer extends, consumer super.

List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>. Wildcards express the particular flexibility an operation needs instead of pretending all lists accept the same additions. List.of creates an unmodifiable list; our output ArrayList is mutable.

Expected output or behavior: 5.0
1
. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Pass an ArrayList<Object> to addOne, then explain why reading its element has type Object. You may trace it without a JDK; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: The wildcard `?` means an unknown type. In `List<? extends Number>`, each item can be read as Number. The exact item type is unknown, so adding an arbitrary non-null number is not safe: the real list may need a different Number child type.

`List<? super Integer>` means the list's item type is Integer or one of its parent types. This view allows adding an Integer. Reading gives only Object, because the list may also hold other kinds of objects.

List<Integer> is not a List<Number>: a list of integers cannot accept every kind of number. Wildcards allow just the flexibility needed. Separately, List.of makes a list that cannot be changed; new ArrayList makes a changeable list.
The program prints 5.0, then 1 on the next line. total adds the input numbers. addOne places one Integer in the output list, whose size becomes one.
The quiz tries to add inside total through its extends view. Java must reject an addition that might not fit the unknown item type, even if a supplied list could be changed.

before.question: Add input.add(1) inside total. Why is the changed program rejected?
choices: An unknown extends subtype cannot safely accept that non-null element
before.explanation: The compile-time wildcard restriction is enough to reject this addition, independently of whether a particular supplied list is mutable.

after.question: Add input.add(1) inside total. Why does compilation fail?
choices: The unknown item type might not accept an Integer.
after.explanation: The extends bound allows reading as Number, but the exact item type is unknown. Java cannot promise that adding an Integer is safe.
